criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban domestic water service access, affordability, and disconnections in Zwelihle township (Hermanus, South Africa) as well as public municipal water and wastewater provision in Toronto, Canada.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it discusses water governance, municipal restructuring, and cost-recovery policy in South Africa and Canada. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it discusses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing access: in Hermanus, the Greater Hermanus Water Conservation Programme (GHWCP) basic charge, free lifeline supply, 11-step increasing block tariff, income-tiered indigent tariff subsidy, and strict credit-control water cut-off enforcement; and in Toronto, a proposal to shift municipal water governance to an arms-length public water board. Plain and narrow readings concur on Criterion 2, so exclusion is driven solely by Criterion 3 (E05), not Criterion 2.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). This is a theoretical urban political ecology essay problematising the concept and multiscalar transfer of environmental justice, illustrated with two short narrative policy overviews of Hermanus and Toronto. The paper contains no methods or data section, no description of fieldwork, sampling, or analytical design, and no primary empirical evidence on service access outcomes (and is not a systematic empirical synthesis). Aside from a single uncontextualised parenthetical quote from a municipal accountant about treating the municipality as a business and one cited 1996 letter, all empirical figures on water demand, revenue, and household cut-offs in Hermanus are drawn from secondary reports (DWAF, 1997b; Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001), while the Toronto section is a narrative account of a defeated 2002 governance proposal citing newspaper and union documents.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses water access, affordability, exclusion from indigent basic-charge subsidies, and household water cut-offs for non-payment in Zwelihle township in Hermanus (citing Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001, that about 60% of residents were affected by cut-offs), though these outcomes are reported via secondary literature rather than primary empirical measurement; no household service access outcome is measured in the Toronto case.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5/7 because no empirical study design, sampling frame, data collection procedure, or empirical unit of observation is reported; population, exposure, and outcome are only sketched narratively from secondary sources to illustrate a theoretical argument on multiscalar environmental justice.

evidence_quotes.quote: We are making two larger theoretical points in this paper. First, we believe that the term ‘environmental justice’ in the context of urban environments must be deﬁned within this context for each site under study; we clearly argue against a universalising use of the term.

Embedded in this paper are two case studies that look speciﬁcally at urban water policy and social justice. First, there is the view from the perspective of equity in access to water in Zwelihle, the Black township in Hermanus, South Africa.

In keeping with DWAF cost recovery policies, the tariff structure of the GHWCP consists of a basic charge for water and a consumption charge which is based on a free lifeline supply followed by an 11-step gradually increasing block tariff.

During this same period, poor communities experienced massive water cut-offs due to non-payment of accounts, as in Zwelihle, where about 60 per cent of residents were affected (Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001).

Throughout this process, a strong labour–community coalition with support from inside the city administration organised and ultimately defeated the attempt to loosen the strong public link of Toronto water and wastewater management.

raw_response.exposure: Greater Hermanus Water Conservation Programme (GHWCP) cost-recovery basic charge, 11-step increasing block tariff, indigent subsidy, and credit-control regime (Hermanus); proposed arms-length municipal water management board (Toronto)
raw_response.outcome: Household water cut-offs for non-payment, non-affordability, and lack of access to indigent tariff subsidies in Zwelihle (reported via secondary literature: Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001); political defeat of proposed water board in Toronto (no access outcome measured)
raw_response.population_and_sample: not reported (no empirical sample; narratively discusses Zwelihle township in Hermanus, South Africa, and the City of Toronto, Canada)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article discusses urban water access and rule-type tariff, cost-recovery, credit-control, and utility-governance mechanisms in Hermanus (South Africa) and Toronto (Canada)—satisfying Criterion 1 and both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2—it is a theoretical political ecology essay problematising the multiscalar concept of environmental justice, illustrated with two brief narrative policy overviews. It has no methods or data section, no identifiable empirical study design or sample, and presents no primary empirical access outcome data (nor is it a systematic empirical synthesis), relying instead on secondary reports (such as DWAF, 1997b, and Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001) for Hermanus water demand and disconnection figures and newspaper/union accounts for the defeated 2002 Toronto governance proposal.
raw_response.study_design: Theoretical urban political ecology essay with narrative policy case overviews (no empirical methods reported)
